title: Entropy Doesn't Mean Getting Messier: Oil and Water Layering and Frost Crystals Are Spontaneous Order
dek: The second law of thermodynamics is often told as "things get messier," but oil separating from water, beach sorting, and window frost are all spontaneous order. Carlo Rovelli says low entropy may not be in the universe but in the way we look at it.
why: This episode has medium-to-high information density. The first half on entropy and time is the most valuable; the second half on AI and free will is more speculative. The ad segment can be skipped.
who: Engineers and researchers interested in time, entropy, and the foundations of quantum mechanics; anyone who wants to hear a physicist dismantle the popular framing that "entropy increase = getting messier."
skip: The Abacus AI ad segment from 34:48 to 36:50 can be skipped.

points.h: Oil separating from water isn't anti-entropy — entropy is producing order
points.body: Rovelli uses a set of everyday images to dismantle the popular framing that "entropy = disorder": water and vinegar mix evenly after being combined, but water and oil separate into layers; fine sand and pebbles sort themselves apart on a beach; frost on a window grows regular structures on its own. He says that under a properly defined notion of "order," many things in nature become spontaneously ordered when left alone. This doesn't overturn the second law — it says popular science draws the correspondence between "order" and "entropy" too crudely. He specifically points out that the complexity of biology and the structure of Earth's surface are often misread as "anti-entropy," when in fact entropy growth itself is constantly producing order.

points.h: Low entropy may not be in the universe but in how you coarse-grain
points.body: Rovelli proposes a hypothesis he has written into a paper but isn't sure is right or wrong: low entropy means "special," but what is special is not the state of the universe — it's coarse graining itself. Coarse graining is a perspective: looking at only some variables, not all the details. If this hypothesis holds, the universe can be in a completely arbitrary state, yet from our perspective, which sees only some variables, it appears low-entropy in the direction we call "the past." This turns the "initial low-entropy boundary condition" from a fact about the universe into a question about how an observer partitions information.

points.h: You can be in two places at once, just not to yourself
points.body: Rovelli pushes quantum superposition onto people: if quantum mechanics is universal, Brian can be in a superposition of Los Angeles and San Francisco, and Carlo can measure that interference. But for Brian himself, quantum mechanics never tells you that you're in a superposition — you look around and see either San Diego or Los Angeles. So "where you are" is two different things for you and for me. He compares this to Galileo discovering that velocity is relative: saying "velocity is zero" actually omits "relative to Earth." What quantum mechanics says is that all properties must be understood relative to something.

points.h: Galileo got the tides wrong using his own relativity principle
points.body: Rovelli uses Galileo's tidal model to show that "having an idea" and "pushing the idea to the end" are two different things. Galileo thought the combination of Earth's revolution around the sun and its rotation stirred the seas, producing tides. But Rovelli points out that revolution is uniform linear motion to first order, and rotation alone can't produce an effect either, so tides can't come from this — what actually explains tides is Newton. Galileo himself violated the very relativity principle he had discovered. Rovelli says Einstein was the same: after writing general relativity in 1915, he later wrote a paper denying gravitational waves (and corrected it after a referee rejected it), and insisted the Schwarzschild singularity was the end of the world — an error he never corrected until his death.

points.h: Without dissipation you can't record anything
points.body: Rovelli says he found a fact in classical mechanics that made him "see the light": if you try to model a measuring device with classical mechanics — a barometer, say, or a device that records whether a ball is on the left or the right — you can't do it unless you introduce dissipation. A ball dropped into a box will bounce; it must dissipate to stop and leave a record. So measurement is essentially a statistical process requiring dissipation, and this was already true before quantum mechanics — it isn't unique to quantum mechanics. This directly answers the puzzle of "unitary evolution is reversible, so where does irreversibility come from": recording itself requires that something be thrown away.

points.h: A chess program deliberates, and so do you
points.body: Rovelli uses his chess computer to dismantle free will: the computer is deterministic — given its internal state and the opponent's move, its output is predetermined. But why does it still spend time enumerating all possible moves and evaluating them one by one? Because the only way to reach that result is to go through this evaluation process, and that process is called deliberation. He says it's stupid to say it isn't deliberating, because deliberation is exactly this. Brian is the same: without going through this complex process, he wouldn't make the decision to start a project or choose a career. So-called freedom is not violating the laws of nature — it is precisely the fact of "having gone through deliberation" itself.

points.h: In principle yes, not now, and within two years he doubts it
points.body: Asked whether machines could have Einstein's "happiest thought" (the equivalence principle in free fall), Rovelli answers in three layers: in principle yes — he doesn't think humans are so special as to be unreproducible; not now; and within two years he's skeptical, but has no hard evidence that it's impossible. He mentions that last week he had Claude do something his PhD student hadn't finished in a month, and Claude did it in half an hour, so the capability is beyond doubt. But he says Claude didn't invent the equivalence principle, and doing that within two years seems hard to him. At the same time he states plainly that there's a lot of hype in AI.

points.h: Ten years and unlimited funding, he'd build a room of Josephson junctions
points.body: Asked what he'd do with "ten years and unlimited funding," Rovelli's answer isn't a telescope or a collider — it's a large room full of Josephson junctions, plus an engineering team. The reason: loop quantum gravity predicts particles of Planck mass, possibly dark matter candidates, with a mass roughly equal to a small piece of hair or a flea egg. He says we already know the direction, mass, and interaction strength of dark matter clouds — only extremely feeble Newtonian gravity, but Josephson junctions could catch it with simple physics. He thinks it's technically feasible within ten years; what's missing is just money.
